tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

1	# Carma shared context
2	
3	Every carma-* skill reads this file first. It is the compact form of the "Carma PoC: Core Design Principles" document plus the constraints agreed with the client. When a skill's output has to choose between options, these principles are the tie-breakers, so cite them by number (P1, P6, ...) in specs.
4	
5	## 1. What we are building
6	
7	A proof of concept for Carma, a media intelligence company that aggregates online content (news, social, broadcast, print) and delivers it to PR and communications clients. The PoC is an **internal tool**. Its job is to **prepare data and make it searchable**. Client-facing presentation, export and sharing come later in the pipeline and are out of scope (see "Deferred" below).
8	
9	## 2. Agreed constraints
10	
11	| Area | Decision |
12	| --- | --- |
13	| Backing store | PostgreSQL. Carma's internal limitations rule out an event-driven platform such as Kafka for now. Queues, retries and processing state therefore live in the database or in-process. |
14	| Volume | About 800 articles per second, roughly 69 million a day. Maximise throughput; capacity is measured against this load. |
15	| Latency target | A brand mention reaches a user within 15 minutes of the article's `published_at` time, for every source and language. Insights are delivered daily or weekly and are not held to this target. |
16	| Priority on conflict | Completeness beats speed. A late item is better than a missed one. Items that miss the target are flagged, not dropped. |
17	| Input data | Articles only: `id`, `headline`, `body`, `source`, `published_at` (UTC timestamp), `language`. Other source types are out of scope. |
18	| Content fidelity | The emphasis is on text content. Storing exact, replicable HTML is not a goal. Headline and body are kept as text and are the system of record. Any markup is reduced to text during validation, and the reduction is recorded as a transformation. Raw markup is not retained by default. A hash of the received payload is kept for integrity and dedupe. |
19	| Deployment | Everything runs under Docker Compose on the target machine: database, web app, workers, observability. `docker compose up` on that machine must set everything up automatically (migrations, roles, extensions, secrets, dashboards). Keys and secrets are handled as configuration, never committed. Compose is single-host, so capacity fit against the 800/s target is checked rather than assumed. |
20	| Languages | English, Arabic and Chinese are in scope for the exercise. Nothing may hard-code those three: any language must work through the same data model. |
21	| Confidence scale | One 0 to 100% scale for every derived field. Scorers usually report on 0 to 1 or another range, so a min/max range is supplied per scoring source and values are normalised. |
22	| Fields needing confidence | Sentiment, relevance, topic, summary, entity match. |
23	| Calibration | Out of scope. Transparency (P7) lets a human or agent decide whether a value is acceptable. |
24	| Evidence base | Carma's public website only. Carma is assumed to agree with the principles. |
25	
26	Illustrative sizing, to be replaced by measurement: 800/s is 48,000 a minute and 2.88 million an hour. The 15-minute window therefore holds about 720,000 articles in flight. At 1 ms of CPU per article the pipeline needs 0.8 cores, at 10 ms it needs 8, at 100 ms it needs 80, so per-article cost is the first thing to question. At 1 to 5 KB of text per article, raw storage is roughly 69 to 345 GB a day before indexes and WAL, so retention and partitioning are first-order design concerns.
27	
28	The sample article in the brief is about 500 characters, shorter than a typical real article. Treat it as a schema example, not a size benchmark.
29	
30	## 3. Principles
31	
32	Use these as design tests: "which principle does this choice serve, and which does it cost?"
33	
34	| # | Principle | In one line | Ask yourself |
35	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
36	| P1 | Fast | Published to visible with minimal delay; clock starts at `published_at` | Is capture lag measured separately from processing time? Can fresh items be searchable before enrichment finishes? |
37	| P2 | Reliable | Predictable; failures are never silent | What happens on crash, retry, duplicate delivery, backlog? Is processing state recorded so work can resume? |
38	| P3 | Complete, honest about gaps | Broad coverage; what is not covered is visible | Can a user tell "no results" from "not covered" from "not yet processed"? Does any path drop an item? |
39	| P4 | Signal over volume | Noise is a defect | Are dedupe/filter/rank decisions recorded so removed content is recoverable? |
40	| P5 | Consistent across markets and languages | Same data model and field definitions everywhere | Does anything assume Latin script, spaces between words, or left-to-right text? |
41	| P6 | Every insight carries a confidence | 0 to 100% on every derived field, visible by default | Does every derived field have a confidence, or an explicit "no confidence available"? |
42	| P7 | Confidence is inspectable | Origin and method stated plainly, even if unimpressive | Do we store origin, method, inputs, raw value, min/max range and normalised value? |
43	| P8 | Everything traces to its source | Any item can be followed back to the original content | Does each derived item reference its source items and the processing applied? |
44	| P9 | Human judgment is part of the system | Automation and people have defined, visible roles | Where can an analyst review, correct or override? Is output marked automated, human-reviewed or human-authored? |
45	| P10 | Data leads to meaning | Explain what happened and why it matters | Does the data model carry the context needed for explanation (topic, entities, sentiment, relationships)? |
46	| P11 | Fit the audience | Content suits the person and situation | Can urgency, audience and market be filtered and derived later? |
47	
48	Priority order when principles conflict: P3 (completeness) outranks P1 (speed) per the client. P2 and P6 to P8 are not traded away for throughput without an explicit decision from the user.
49	
50	### Confidence model (P6, P7)
51	
52	Every derived value stores: the normalised confidence (0 to 100), the raw score, the min/max range of the scoring source, the origin type, the method and its version, and when it was produced. Origins we expect: model self-report (an LLM stating "60% confident"), rule-based, statistical or classifier score, human review, combined. A 60 from a model's self-report and a 60 from a classifier mean different things, so the origin always travels with the number. Never present a self-reported LLM figure as a statistical probability.
53	
54	### Deferred (do not design for now)
55	
56	Shareable-by-default outputs: executive briefings, branded newsletters, ready-made reports, exports. Keep data models from making these harder later (P11), nothing more.
57	
58	## 4. Known unknowns
59	
60	These are unverified. If a design depends on one, say so in the spec and ask.
61	
62	- `published_at` is source-supplied and assumed accurate. Missing, future-dated or wrong values would corrupt the 15-minute clock.
63	- Whether `id` is globally unique or only unique per source.
64	- Whether bodies arrive as plain text or HTML (the sample is plain text). Original markup is assumed not needed for now; revisit if a requirement changes.
65	- Target machine specs (CPU, memory, disk, OS), whether it has internet access to pull images, and whether images are built in CI or on the target.
66	- Real average article size, source mix and language mix.
67	- PostgreSQL version, hosting model and which extensions are permitted in Carma's environment.
68	- Which brand or query sets drive "brand mention" detection, and how many standing queries exist.
69	
70	## 5. Spec conventions (when run inside a codebase)
71	
72	Skills write their output as numbered markdown files so decisions and reasoning survive the conversation and later skills can read them.
73	
74	| Skill | Output directory |
75	| --- | --- |
76	| carma-architect (raw design docs) | `.specs/architect/` |
77	| carma-architect (approved decisions) | `.specs/architect/adrs/` |
78	| carma-searchability | `.specs/search/` |
79	| carma-telemetry | `.specs/telemetry/` |
80	| carma-data-sanity | `.specs/data/sanitization/` |
81	| carma-dba | `.specs/data/dba/` |
82	| carma-backend-testing | `.specs/testing/backend/` |
83	| carma-devops | `.specs/devops/` |
84	| carma-ux | `.specs/ux/` |
85	| carma-review (runs outside the main flow) | `.specs/review/` |
86	| carma-benchmark (runs outside the main flow) | `.benchmarks/<feature>/` (executable Node.js files, not numbered specs) |
87	| carma-plan | `.specs/plan/` |
88	
89	**"In a codebase" means** the working directory is a project: it has a `.git` directory or a recognisable manifest (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, `pom.xml`, `Cargo.toml`, `*.csproj`, etc.) or a source tree. If it is not, do not create files. Deliver the output in the conversation and offer to save it once a project is available.
90	
91	**Numbering.** Each directory has its own sequence of four-digit numbers: `0001-short-slug.md`, `0002-...`. Get the next number with `scripts/next_spec_number.py <directory>`, which also creates the directory if it is missing. Never reuse or renumber a file. Edit a spec in place while its status is `draft`; once it is `approved`, a change is a new file whose front matter says `supersedes`.
92	
93	**Front matter** on every spec:
94	
95	```yaml
96	---
97	spec: carma-dba            # skill that produced it
98	number: 0003
99	title: Partitioned storage for article ingestion
100	status: draft              # draft | in-review | approved | superseded
101	date: 2026-10-24
102	feature: article-ingestion # short name shared across the specs for one feature
103	inputs: [.specs/architect/0002-article-ingestion.md]
104	principles: [P1, P2, P3]
105	supersedes: null
106	---
107	```
108	
109	**Finding inputs.** Upstream specs for the same `feature` are the input. List the relevant directory, read the highest-numbered non-superseded spec for that feature (plus any ADRs that reference it), and record the paths under `inputs`. If an expected input is missing, say so and either run the upstream skill's analysis inline or ask the user, rather than guessing.
110	
111	## 6. When to ask the user
112	
113	Ask when a requirement is ambiguous, when two priorities conflict and the principles above do not settle it, or when a choice is expensive to reverse. Do not ask what the constraints above already answer, and do not ask what you can find by reading the codebase.
114	
115	Ask with the AskUserQuestion tool when it is available (one to four questions, two to four options each, recommended option first and marked). Each option needs its trade-off in one line: what it gains, what it costs, which principles it touches. If the tool is not available, ask in plain text with the same structure. If nobody is available to answer (an unattended or scheduled run), pick the option that best matches the principles, mark it `UNCONFIRMED` in the spec, and list it under open questions so it is not mistaken for a decision.
116	
117	Group questions: one round of well-formed questions beats a stream of single ones.
118

# carma-architect

Turn a feature requirement into a design that fits the code that already exists and the principles Carma cares about. Everything downstream (searchability, DBA, telemetry, data sanity, testing, UX, planning) reads your output, so it has to be specific enough to act on and honest about what is unknown.

Read `references/carma-context.md` before anything else. It holds the principles (P1 to P11), the agreed constraints (PostgreSQL only, about 800 articles a second, 15 minutes from `published_at`, completeness over speed) and the spec conventions. Cite principles by number in your output so the reasoning can be checked. When a design could use PostgreSQL extensions (queues, vectors, partition automation, search), also read `references/postgres-extensions.md`.

## Workflow

### 1. Intake: restate the requirement

Restate the requirement in your own words, split into functional needs and non-functional needs (latency, volume, languages, confidence, audience). For each, note which principles it touches. Collect ambiguities in a list but do not ask yet; most become answerable once you have seen the code.

Skip questions the context file already answers. The constraints there are decided, so build on them instead of reopening them.

### 2. Analyse the codebase

Look before you design. A design that ignores the existing structure creates rework, and one that duplicates something already built wastes the team's time. If the repository is large, delegate the sweep to an Explore agent and ask for the conclusion, not file dumps.

Find and record, with file paths as evidence:

- **Shape.** Languages, frameworks, module boundaries, entry points, how the application is deployed and configured.
- **Ingestion path.** How articles arrive today, what validates them, where they are first persisted.
- **Data layer.** Schema, migrations, ORM or raw SQL, indexes, partitioning, connection handling, PostgreSQL version if discoverable.
- **Extensions.** Which are already enabled or installed (`CREATE EXTENSION` in migrations, container images, infrastructure code, `pg_available_extensions` if the database is reachable) and what the hosting environment permits. Unknown availability is a finding, not something to assume away.
- **Async work.** Jobs, workers, schedulers, any queue-like tables, retry behaviour. Remember there is no Kafka.
- **Enrichment.** Anything that calls an LLM or scorer, how confidence is produced and stored today.
- **Search.** Current query paths, full-text setup, language handling.
- **Observability.** Logging, metrics, tracing, health checks (carma-telemetry goes deeper; just note what exists).
- **Tests and CI.** Frameworks, coverage of the pipeline, load or integration tests.
- **Conventions.** Naming, layering, error handling, anything a new feature must follow.

If there is no code yet, say so. Greenfield changes the questions (you choose structure instead of adapting to it) but not the principles.

State what you could not determine. "Postgres version unknown" is more useful than a silent assumption.

### 3. Design

Propose the architecture that satisfies the requirement with the least disruption to what exists. For each significant decision, develop at least two real options (not a straw man), then recommend one and say why.

Lenses to apply, because they are where Carma pipelines tend to go wrong:

- **Throughput arithmetic.** At 800 articles a second, per-article cost dominates. Estimate cost per stage and compare to the budget in the context file. A synchronous call per article to a slow service is a design smell at this rate; batching, tiering (cheap checks first, expensive enrichment on a subset) and backpressure usually matter more than micro-optimisation.
- **Postgres as the backbone.** With no event platform, the database carries queues, state and results. Consider work claiming with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, an explicit per-item processing-state table, append-only writes instead of in-place updates, batch inserts, and keeping the hot write path light. Flag where the proposed load could contend with search reads. carma-dba will detail this; your job is to choose the shape.
- **Extensions as design options.** Postgres extensions can deliver reliability and searchability with little code: queue semantics with visibility timeouts and transactional enqueue (P2), vector search for meaning-based and cross-language matching and story clustering (P3, P5, P10), partition automation and scheduling, CJK-capable text search. Evaluate them using `references/postgres-extensions.md`: confirm availability, say which principle each serves and what it costs on the write path, and always keep a core-Postgres fallback in the design. A vector index supplements lexical matching for brand mentions; it never replaces it, because approximate search can miss (P3). Adopting an extension is a decision for the user, not a default.
- **Fresh before rich (P1, P3).** Items should become findable as soon as they land, with enrichment arriving afterwards. Design explicit states ("captured", "searchable", "enriched") so users and operators can tell them apart.
- **No silent loss (P2, P3).** Trace every way an article could be dropped, duplicated or stuck. Every exit from the pipeline needs a recorded reason.
- **Confidence and lineage (P6, P7, P8).** Wherever a value is derived, the design must say where confidence, origin, method and source references are stored.
- **Language neutrality (P5).** Nothing in the design may assume English, whitespace tokenisation or left-to-right text.
- **Human touchpoints (P9).** Mark where an analyst reviews or overrides.
- **Resilience (P2, P3).** Every dependency the pipeline calls (source feeds, scorers and LLMs, the database, object stores, other services) will be slow, wrong or down at some point. Design the response deliberately, per dependency, and record it in the "Resilience design" section. See `Resilience design` below.
- **Benchmarkability.** Quick benchmarks (carma-benchmark) are how we prove completeness and speed after each change, so design for them. Keep hot-path logic callable without the whole service (pure functions or small modules with explicit inputs), make the clock, random source and external dependencies replaceable at a seam, expose counters that let a run verify `received = accounted for`, and give the benchmark a way to run against a disposable database. If a requirement cannot be benchmarked, say why and what would make it so. Where a design choice makes benchmarking much harder, treat that as a cost in the trade-off.
- **Deployability.** Everything runs under Docker Compose on one host and must come up from a single `docker compose up`. Name every component that must run (database, workers, web app, observability), the settings and secrets each needs, and whether the capacity target fits one machine. carma-devops details this.
- **Reversibility.** Prefer designs that can be changed later. Flag one-way doors.

#### Resilience design

For each dependency and each stage boundary, decide and write down:

- **Failure classification.** Transient (timeouts, connection resets, 429 and 5xx, deadlocks, serialisation failures, brief failovers), permanent (malformed or missing source, 4xx other than 429, authentication or authorisation rejected, schema mismatch, content the scorer always rejects), and ambiguous (treat as transient for a bounded number of attempts, then as permanent). Retrying a permanent failure only burns capacity, and giving up on a transient one loses data, so the classifier is a design element in its own right and needs tests.
- **Retry strategy.** Which operations retry, how many attempts, exponential backoff with jitter (to avoid synchronised retry storms at 800 articles a second), a per-attempt timeout and an overall deadline tied to the 15-minute window, and a retry budget that caps retries as a share of traffic. Retries must be safe: only idempotent operations retry automatically, with idempotency keys or natural keys where an operation is not naturally idempotent. Decide whether retries live in the caller or in the database queue (attempt count, next-attempt time, last error, visible in the ledger).
- **Circuit breaker.** For each remote dependency, when the breaker opens (error rate or consecutive failures over a window, or latency over a threshold), how it half-opens with limited probes, how it closes, and per-dependency scope so one bad source or scorer does not trip the rest. State what the system does while it is open: queue the work durably, skip optional enrichment and mark the item "not yet enriched", or fall back to a cheaper method. State clearly what must not happen: dropping the item, or showing a default as if it were a result (P3, P6).
- **Bulkheads and limits.** Separate worker pools, connection pools and concurrency limits per dependency so a slow scorer cannot exhaust the connections the ingestion path needs; bounded queues and timeouts everywhere; backpressure rather than unbounded memory growth.
- **Permanent-failure handling.** After the attempt limit or on a permanent classification, the item moves to a dead-letter or quarantine state with the reason, attempts, last error and timestamps. It stays visible, can be replayed after the cause is fixed, and counts in the reconciliation totals. A permanently unreachable source produces a visible coverage gap (P3), not silence.
- **Degraded modes.** What a user sees when a dependency is down: items searchable without enrichment, confidence shown as "no confidence available", freshness and coverage banners. Late items are flagged as late.
- **Recovery.** Catch-up must outrun arrival; replay is rate-limited so recovery does not become the next outage; breakers close gradually.
- **Poison-item and loop protection.** A bounded attempt count per item and per stage, so one article cannot cycle forever (cost controls are detailed in carma-data-sanity).

Where the decision is a real trade-off (for example how long to keep retrying inside the 15-minute window before declaring a mention late, or whether to queue or skip during an outage), put it to the user.

### 4. Trade-offs and user decisions

When something is unclear, or two priorities conflict and the principles do not settle it, stop and put the choice to the user. Do not bury a consequential choice inside the design. Follow the "When to ask the user" protocol in the context file: grouped questions, options with their cost and benefit in a line, a recommendation first.

Typical triggers: build versus extend an existing component, a schema change that is hard to reverse, throughput versus durability settings, enrichment cost versus coverage, a requirement that conflicts with a principle, scope that the requirement leaves open, and whether to adopt a Postgres extension (offer packages: core only, core plus operational basics, extended; see the extensions reference).

Record every open choice in the spec under "Decisions needed", with its options, whichever way it is resolved.

### 5. Points of failure register

List the ways the feature can fail or silently go wrong. This register becomes the focus of the testing skill, so write entries a tester can turn into test cases.

| ID | Failure point | Failure mode and effect | Principle at risk | How we would detect it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FP-1 | e.g. Worker crashes after claiming a batch | Articles stuck "in progress" forever, mentions missed | P2, P3 | Claim age metric, stuck-item sweeper |

Cover at least: ingestion (bad or missing fields, duplicates, out-of-order or late arrival), state transitions, retries and poison items, database saturation and failover, enrichment dependency failures, backlog and catch-up, clock and timestamp issues, language and encoding edge cases, and anything where an item can disappear without a recorded reason.

### 6. Hot path register

Identify the code paths that run per article or per query at volume, or that touch shared contended resources. These need extra human attention or manual inspection, and they are the input for the performance skill that follows.

| ID | Path | Why it is hot | Expected load | What needs a human | Suggested measurement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HP-1 | e.g. Batch insert into the articles table | Every article passes through, index maintenance multiplies cost | 800 rows/s sustained | Review index set and batch size against the write budget | Rows/s and p99 commit time under sustained load |

"What needs a human" is the important column. Say specifically what judgment a person must apply (review a query plan, inspect a regex, decide a batch size, approve a timeout), not just "review this".

### 7. Telemetry starting points

List the signals this design needs so the infra team can hold the reliability and performance targets and developers can debug special cases. Keep it to starting points; carma-telemetry builds the full plan.

Always include: end-to-end freshness measured from `published_at`, capture lag versus processing time per stage, throughput in and out per stage, queue depth and oldest-item age, reconciliation counts (received = accounted for, by outcome and reason), error and retry rates, and one signal per entry in the failure register.

### 8. Downstream handoff

State which follow-on skills apply and what each needs from this spec:

- **carma-searchability**: applies if any requirement involves querying the data. Say what is searched and how often.
- **carma-data-sanity**: applies if untrusted content is ingested or sent to an LLM, which is nearly always.
- **carma-dba**: applies if storage, indexes or write paths change. Tell it which extensions the design leans on and the fallback, so it can verify availability and cost.
- **carma-telemetry**: applies to any feature that runs in production.
- **carma-ux**: applies if a person sees or interacts with the result.
- **carma-devops**: applies to anything that must be deployed or run, which is nearly always. Give it the components, settings, secrets and capacity numbers.
- **carma-backend-testing**: applies once the design and database plans exist. It turns the FP register and the resilience design into negative, fault and recovery tests.
- **carma-plan**: last, to combine everything.
- **carma-benchmark** and **carma-review** run outside this flow, after code changes. Tell them which HP entries deserve a benchmark and which paths must stay simple for human review.

## Output

Write the spec with these sections, in this order, so downstream skills know where to look:

1. **Summary** (the design in a short paragraph and the main decision it asks for)
2. **Requirements digest** (functional, non-functional, principles touched)
3. **Codebase findings** (with paths; unknowns listed)
4. **Proposed architecture** (components, data flow, states, where confidence and lineage live; a diagram in text or Mermaid where it helps)
5. **Options considered** (per significant decision: options, trade-offs, recommendation; include any extension candidates with availability status, principle served, cost and core fallback)
6. **Decisions needed** (open choices for the user, each with options and recommendation)
7. **Points of failure** (FP register)
8. **Resilience design** (table per dependency: failure classes, retry policy, circuit breaker, bulkhead, permanent-failure handling, degraded mode)
9. **Hot paths** (HP register)
10. **Telemetry starting points** (include breaker state, retry counts, dead-letter depth)
11. **Principle alignment** (table: principle, how the design serves it, what it costs)
12. **Downstream handoff** (which skills, what they need)
13. **Open questions and assumptions** (mark unconfirmed assumptions `UNCONFIRMED`)

## Persisting the work (when run inside a codebase)

See "Spec conventions" in the context file for what counts as a codebase, front matter and numbering.

1. **Raw design doc.** Get the number with `python scripts/next_spec_number.py .specs/architect` and write `.specs/architect/NNNN-<feature-slug>.md` with `spec: carma-architect` front matter and `status: draft`. This is the full output above, written before any decision is codified.
2. **ADRs after human decisions.** When the user decides an open choice or approves the plan, record each decision as its own numbered ADR in `.specs/architect/adrs/` (number with `python scripts/next_spec_number.py .specs/architect/adrs`). One decision per ADR. Only write ADRs for decisions a human has actually made or approved; an `UNCONFIRMED` default is not a decision.
3. **Link them.** Add the ADR numbers to the raw doc under a "Decisions recorded" heading, and set `status: approved` once the user approves the design. Each ADR points back to the raw doc.

If the repository already keeps ADRs somewhere else (for example `docs/adr`), ask the user whether to follow that convention or use `.specs/architect/adrs`. Do not scatter ADRs across two places.

If you are not in a codebase, deliver the output in the conversation and offer to save it.

### ADR format (MADR-style)

```markdown
---
adr: 0003
title: Claim enrichment work with SKIP LOCKED in Postgres
status: accepted          # proposed | accepted | superseded | rejected
date: 2026-10-24
decision-makers: [name or role]
raw-spec: ../0002-article-ingestion.md

---

## Context and problem statement
What forced the decision, in two or three sentences. Link the requirement and the constraint that bites (for example, no event platform).

## Decision drivers
- P2 reliable: work must survive worker crashes
- Throughput: 800 articles/s sustained

## Considered options
1. Option A
2. Option B
3. Option C

## Decision outcome
Chosen option: "Option B", because it best satisfies the drivers above.

### Consequences
- Good: ...

- Risks and how we will notice them: link FP/HP entries

### Confirmation
How we will know it works: tests (FP-n), telemetry signals, measurements (HP-n).

## Pros and cons of the options
Short, honest list per option.
```

## Quality bar

Before finishing, check: every significant claim about the codebase cites a path; every FP and HP entry is specific enough to test or measure; every principle is either served or its cost is named; open questions are marked rather than hidden inside the design. A design that reads as certain about things nobody has verified is worse than one that lists its unknowns.

## Context and problem statement

# ADR-0001: Size to the assignment scope, keep a documented path to Carma scale

## Context and problem statement
The home assignment asks for a small service (20 sample articles, an LLM cost case of 50,000 articles a day, 7 to 9 hours, "don't gold-plate"). The shared Carma context assumes 800 articles a second and a 15-minute freshness target from `published_at`. Designing for both literally is impossible in the time budget, and the brief grades decisions and trade-offs, not completeness.

## Decision drivers
- Grading rewards reasoned trade-offs over completeness (PDF, "Don't gold-plate").
- P2, P3 and P5 to P8 should still hold, so the design can grow.
- 800 articles a second would require partitioning, bulk-write tuning and load tests that the brief does not ask for.

## Considered options
1. Assignment scope, Carma-ready: build for 20 articles and the 50K-a-day cost case; keep schema and component boundaries so the 800/s target and the 15-minute SLO are a documented growth path.
2. Full Carma scale now.
3. Assignment scope only, ignoring Carma constraints.

## Decision outcome
Chosen option: "Assignment scope, Carma-ready", because it meets the grading criteria within the time budget while keeping the Carma principles checkable.

### Consequences
- Good: small, finishable plan; a README section can describe the growth path with evidence.
- Good: structure (job ledger, transactional enqueue, append-only enrichments, content hash) is the same shape needed at scale.
- Bad: partitioning, bulk-insert tuning, pgmq/pgvector and the 15-minute SLO measurement are documented but not built.
- Risks: the growth path claims are untested at scale. Mitigation: a quick synthetic benchmark of HP-2, HP-3 and HP-4 on a larger table (optional, carma-benchmark).

### Confirmation
README "Architecture & Decisions" lists what is built, what is stubbed and how it would be finished; plan phases show the cut line.

## Pros and cons of the options
1. Meets the brief and the principles; some claims are untested at scale.
2. Faithful to Carma; blows the time budget and risks gold-plating.
3. Smallest; abandons the shared principles and traceability.

## 1. Summary
Add a web upload (page plus `POST /api/uploads`) that takes a JSON array of articles, runs each through the existing validate, sanitise and insert path (`loadArticles`), which already queues the `sentiment` and `summary_topics` enrichment jobs the worker picks up. The file is never sent whole to an LLM; each article is enriched individually under the ADR-0010 budget. The request returns a per-article outcome report keyed by a `batch_id`, and a second endpoint lets the page follow each article from `admitted` to `enriched`.

The main decision: the web service today only holds the read-only `app_read` credential, so an upload route needs a write path (D1).

## 2. Requirements digest
Functional
- F1 Upload a JSON file (array of `{id, headline, body, source, published_at, language}`) from the UI or API.
- F2 Each article goes through the same pipeline as the seed loader: validate, reduce markup, insert, enqueue enrichment.
- F3 Return a report: received, admitted, duplicate, quarantined with reason codes, per article position.
- F4 Show enrichment progress for the batch (queued, running, deferred for budget, done, dead).

Non-functional
- N1 No silent loss: every array element ends in `ingest_events` with an outcome (P2, P3).
- N2 Idempotent re-upload of the same file (P2).
- N3 Spend stays bounded by ADR 0010; upload cannot bypass it (P2).
- N4 Any language through the same model (P5).
- N5 Upload data is untrusted (carma-data-sanity).

## 3. Codebase findings
- `src/lib/ingest/ingest.ts` `loadArticles(items, batchKind, pool?, config?)` already does everything per item, with a pool and config that can be injected. One transaction per item, a `batch_id` per call, outcomes `admitted | duplicate | quarantined | error`, duplicate by `(source, external_id)`, content duplicates flagged only. It returns counts only (no per-item list), and it is sequential (about 4 queries per item).
- `ingestOne` inserts `enrichment_jobs` for `sentiment` and `summary_topics` in the same transaction as the article (transactional enqueue, P2).
- `src/lib/validate/article.ts` caps one item at 1 MiB and rejects with reason codes; `src/cli/load.ts` is the only current caller (CLI, `ROLE=seed`).
- `loadArticlesFile` requires the top-level value to be an array and throws otherwise.
- `compose.yaml` web service uses `DB_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/app_read_password`; container is `read_only` with `cap_drop: ALL`. `ops/init-secrets.sh` copies `app_ingest_password` only to `migrate` and `seed`. Role grants (`db/migrations/0001_init.sql` lines 224-250): `app_ingest` has SELECT/INSERT on articles and INSERT on events, quarantine, transformations and jobs; `app_read` is SELECT only with a 2s statement timeout.
- Existing routes live in `src/app/api/*/route.ts` (Route Handlers). There is no auth, no `proxy.ts`/middleware, and no existing write endpoint.
- Worker (`src/worker/*`) claims `enrichment_jobs`, with budget (`budget.ts`), breaker and retry already in place.
- Not determined: reverse proxy body limits on the target host; Next route handler body size behaviour in this version (read `node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/03-file-conventions/route.md` and `01-app/01-getting-started/15-route-handlers.md` before coding).

## 4. Proposed architecture
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  UI[Upload page] -->|multipart file| API[POST /api/uploads]
  CLI[curl] --> API
  API -->|guard: token, size, count| V[parse JSON array]
  V -->|per item| ING[loadArticles with ingest pool]
  ING --> PG[(articles, ingest_events, quarantine, enrichment_jobs)]
  PG --> W[worker: claim, budget, breaker, provider]
  W --> PG
  UI -->|poll| ST[GET /api/uploads/:batchId]
  ST --> PG
```
Components
- `POST /api/uploads` (new route handler). Checks the shared upload token, content length against `UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES`, parses the file, rejects a non-array or an over-limit item count (`UPLOAD_MAX_ITEMS`) with 4xx and no rows written, then calls `loadArticles(items, "backfill", ingestPool, cfg)`. `backfill` keeps uploads out of the live freshness watermark (P3 honesty: not a live batch).
- `loadArticles` change: also return a per-item result list `{position, outcome, reason_codes, article_id}` (the data is already written to `ingest_events`). Keep the pure function shape (benchmarkable).
- `GET /api/uploads/:batchId` (new): reads `ingest_events` for the batch joined to `enrichment_jobs` states; read-only, can use the existing `app_read` pool (needs SELECT on `ingest_events` for `app_read`; today only `app_ingest` has it, so a one-line grant migration `0003`).
- Upload page (carma-ux): file picker, token field, report table, progress per article.
- Ingest pool in the web process: separate `createPool(...,"web-ingest")` with `app_ingest` credentials, used only by the upload route (D1).
- One in-flight upload per web instance (semaphore, 429 otherwise) so the ingest pool cannot starve search reads.

States per article: `received` (event) then `admitted | duplicate | quarantined`; admitted articles are searchable immediately (fresh before rich, P1) and enrichment jobs move `queued` to `done`, `deferred_budget` or `dead`.

Confidence and lineage: unchanged. Enrichment continues to write confidence, origin and method (P6, P7); each article traces to its upload through `ingest_events.batch_id` and `payload_sha256` (P8). Add `batch_kind`/source label `upload` only if D4 (not needed now) is accepted; otherwise the `batch_id` is the lineage.

Human touchpoint (P9): quarantined items from an upload appear in the existing quarantine review surface with their `batch_id`.

## 5. Options considered
O1 Where the write credential lives
1. Second pool in web using `app_ingest` (recommended): smallest change; mounts one more secret into web. Cost: web can now insert articles and events if compromised.
2. Dedicated ingest service/container with its own port, web proxies to it: strongest isolation, extra service, Compose change, more to run. Over the ADR 0001 scope.
3. Web stages the raw file into a table and a worker ingests it: keeps web read-only except one staging grant, adds new table, worker stage, and delays visibility (P1 cost).

O2 Sync vs async processing of the file
1. Synchronous in the request, bounded by caps (recommended): at about 4 queries per item, 1,000 items is a few to tens of seconds; the caller gets the full report. Cost: long request, ties up the ingest pool.
2. Accept (202) and process in the web process in background: route returns fast, but work is lost on restart and no recovery (P2).
3. Stage and process in a worker (see O1.3): durable, more build.

O3 Authentication
1. Shared upload token from a secret (`UPLOAD_TOKEN_FILE`), constant-time compare (recommended): the only write endpoint should not be open, and it spends LLM budget. Cost: token handling in the UI.
2. No auth, like the rest of the app: simplest, but anyone reaching the port can add data and spend budget.

O4 Idempotency and duplicates (no decision needed): reuse `(source, external_id)` skip plus content-hash flag; re-uploading the same file yields all `duplicate`, zero new jobs.

O5 Extensions: none needed. Core Postgres only.

## 6. Decisions needed
- D1 Write credential for the upload route: option 1 (second `app_ingest` pool in web), 2 (separate ingest service), or 3 (stage then worker). Recommend 1.
- D2 Processing model: sync bounded (recommend), or stage and worker. Linked to D1.
- D3 Authentication: shared token (recommend) or none.
- UNCONFIRMED defaults: `UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES=5 MiB`, `UPLOAD_MAX_ITEMS=1000`, uploads recorded as `backfill`, one upload at a time per instance.

## 7. Points of failure
| ID | Failure point | Mode and effect | Principle | Detection |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FP-1 | File is not valid JSON or not an array | Whole file rejected 400, nothing written; must say why | P3 | 4xx metric, report body |
| FP-2 | Oversized file or too many items | 413/422 before any write; no partial acceptance | P2 | reject counter by reason |
| FP-3 | Element invalid or non-object | Quarantined with reason code, others continue; position preserved | P3 | `ingest_events` count vs received |
| FP-4 | DB connection drops mid-file | Request fails after some items committed; caller must be able to resume safely | P2 | 5xx; re-upload is idempotent (N2) |
| FP-5 | Client disconnects mid-request | Server continues or aborts partway; batch partly applied without a report | P2 | batch event count vs expected; GET batch shows actual |
| FP-6 | Same file uploaded twice or concurrently | Concurrent identical items race on `(source, external_id)`; ON CONFLICT handles it, one admitted, one duplicate | P2 | duplicate count |
| FP-7 | Upload floods the LLM budget | 1,000 items queue jobs; budget caps spend and defers; lag shown | P2, ADR 0010 | deferred_budget count, budget banner |
| FP-8 | Upload starves search reads | Long upload holds the ingest pool and CPU | P1 | pool wait time, search p95 |
| FP-9 | Token missing/leaked/logged | Unauthorised writes; token in logs | security | 401 counter; log scrub test |
| FP-10 | Hostile article text (markup, injection, huge values, NULs, lone surrogates) | Existing sanitise/validate and ADR 0012 apply; unsafe items flagged | P2 | flags; sanity tests |
| FP-11 | Upload counted as live batch | Corrupts freshness watermark | P3 | batch_kind = backfill assertion |
| FP-12 | Outcome mismatch: received != admitted + duplicate + quarantined | Silent drop | P3 | per-request reconciliation, asserted in response and test |

## 8. Resilience design
| Dependency | Failure classes | Retry | Breaker | Bulkhead | Permanent failures | Degraded mode |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres (ingest pool) | transient: connection reset, 57P01/57P03, deadlock; permanent: constraint/validation (already quarantined per item) | No automatic retry inside the request; the caller re-sends (idempotent, FP-4). Per-item deadlock retry once is acceptable | None (pool errors surface as 503) | Separate ingest pool, one upload at a time, UPLOAD_MAX_ITEMS | Item errors recorded as `ingest_error` quarantine | 503 with `Retry-After`; reads keep working on the read pool |
| LLM providers | unchanged: worker retry, breaker and budget (ADR 0010, existing `src/worker/*`) | existing | existing | existing worker concurrency | dead-letter existing | Articles searchable, enrichment shows queued/deferred, confidence "none yet" |
| Client | disconnect, slow upload | none | n/a | request timeout and body limit | n/a | Partial effects visible through `GET /api/uploads/:batchId` |

## 9. Hot paths
| ID | Path | Why hot | Expected load | What needs a human | Measurement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HP-1 | `ingestOne` per upload item | 4+ queries per item, sequential | up to 1,000 items per request | Decide batch limits and whether to batch inserts after measuring; inspect transaction scope | items/s and request p95 for 1,000 items on the small DB profile |
| HP-2 | JSON parse of up to 5 MiB in the web process | Blocks the event loop | one at a time | Confirm limit vs memory limit of the container (mem_limit in compose) | peak RSS, event-loop lag |
| HP-3 | Batch status query | Join events to jobs for a batch | polling every few seconds | Review plan on `events_batch_idx` | query p95 |

carma-benchmark candidates: HP-1 (completeness `received = accounted for`, plus throughput).

## 10. Telemetry starting points
`upload_requests_total{outcome}`, `upload_rejected_total{reason}`, `upload_items_total{outcome}`, `upload_duration_seconds`, ingest pool wait/usage, in-flight upload gauge, 401/429 counts, batch reconciliation mismatch counter (must stay 0), deferred_budget jobs for upload batches, event-loop lag, plus existing worker, queue age and breaker signals. Log batch_id, byte size, item count, never the file contents or token.

## 11. Principle alignment
| Principle | Serves | Costs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P1 | Admitted articles searchable before enrichment | Sync upload holds the request |
| P2 | Per-item transactions, transactional enqueue, idempotent re-upload | No resumable upload; caller re-sends |
| P3 | Every element has an outcome, whole-file rejects are loud | Upload caps may refuse legitimate big files |
| P6/P7/P8 | Unchanged enrichment confidence, batch_id lineage | None |
| P9 | Quarantine review covers uploads | Review UI scope unchanged |

## 12. Downstream handoff
- carma-searchability: no new query needs; uploaded articles are searchable through existing paths. Run only if routing wants confirmation. Skip suggested.
- carma-data-sanity: apply. Untrusted file: size and count caps, content-type, JSON depth, filename handling, injection into LLM (ADR 0012), token handling.
- carma-dba: small. Grant `SELECT` on `ingest_events` to `app_read` (or a status function), ingest pool in web, per-batch index check; possibly a `status_batch(batch_id)` SQL function.
- carma-telemetry: apply (section 10).
- carma-ux: apply. Upload page, report table, per-article progress.
- carma-devops: apply. Mount `app_ingest_password` and `UPLOAD_TOKEN` secret into web (`ops/init-secrets.sh`, `compose.yaml`), request body limits, container memory.
- carma-backend-testing: apply (FP-1..FP-12, reconciliation, idempotent re-upload, fault injection on the DB).
- carma-plan: last.
- carma-benchmark after code: HP-1. carma-review: keep `ingestOne` untouched and the route handler thin.

## 13. Open questions and assumptions
- UNCONFIRMED: caps 5 MiB / 1,000 items; `backfill` kind; single in-flight upload; token auth.
- UNCONFIRMED: whether Next.js route handlers in this version stream or buffer `request.formData()` and its default size limits (check docs before coding).
- Is the upload meant for operators only (internal) or for external clients? Affects D3.
- Should an upload file be retained after processing? Assumed no (only per-item payload hashes, quarantine payload per ADR 0011).

# 0002 Upload a JSON articles file through the ingest and enrichment flow

## 1. Summary
Add a web upload (page plus `POST /api/uploads`) that takes a JSON array of articles, runs each through the existing validate, sanitise and insert path (`loadArticles`), which already queues the `sentiment` and `summary_topics` enrichment jobs the worker picks up. The file is never sent whole to an LLM; each article is enriched individually under the ADR-0010 budget. The request returns a per-article outcome report keyed by a `batch_id`, and a second endpoint lets the page follow each article from `admitted` to `enriched`.

The main decision: the web service today only holds the read-only `app_read` credential, so an upload route needs a write path (D1).

## 2. Requirements digest
Functional
- F1 Upload a JSON file (array of `{id, headline, body, source, published_at, language}`) from the UI or API.
- F2 Each article goes through the same pipeline as the seed loader: validate, reduce markup, insert, enqueue enrichment.
- F3 Return a report: received, admitted, duplicate, quarantined with reason codes, per article position.
- F4 Show enrichment progress for the batch (queued, running, deferred for budget, done, dead).

Non-functional
- N1 No silent loss: every array element ends in `ingest_events` with an outcome (P2, P3).
- N2 Idempotent re-upload of the same file (P2).
- N3 Spend stays bounded by ADR 0010; upload cannot bypass it (P2).
- N4 Any language through the same model (P5).
- N5 Upload data is untrusted (carma-data-sanity).

## 3. Codebase findings
- `src/lib/ingest/ingest.ts` `loadArticles(items, batchKind, pool?, config?)` already does everything per item, with a pool and config that can be injected. One transaction per item, a `batch_id` per call, outcomes `admitted | duplicate | quarantined | error`, duplicate by `(source, external_id)`, content duplicates flagged only. It returns counts only (no per-item list), and it is sequential (about 4 queries per item).
- `ingestOne` inserts `enrichment_jobs` for `sentiment` and `summary_topics` in the same transaction as the article (transactional enqueue, P2).
- `src/lib/validate/article.ts` caps one item at 1 MiB and rejects with reason codes; `src/cli/load.ts` is the only current caller (CLI, `ROLE=seed`).
- `loadArticlesFile` requires the top-level value to be an array and throws otherwise.
- `compose.yaml` web service uses `DB_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/app_read_password`; container is `read_only` with `cap_drop: ALL`. `ops/init-secrets.sh` copies `app_ingest_password` only to `migrate` and `seed`. Role grants (`db/migrations/0001_init.sql` lines 224-250): `app_ingest` has SELECT/INSERT on articles and INSERT on events, quarantine, transformations and jobs; `app_read` is SELECT only with a 2s statement timeout.
- Existing routes live in `src/app/api/*/route.ts` (Route Handlers). There is no auth, no `proxy.ts`/middleware, and no existing write endpoint.
- Worker (`src/worker/*`) claims `enrichment_jobs`, with budget (`budget.ts`), breaker and retry already in place.
- Not determined: reverse proxy body limits on the target host; Next route handler body size behaviour in this version (read `node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/03-file-conventions/route.md` and `01-app/01-getting-started/15-route-handlers.md` before coding).

## 4. Proposed architecture
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  UI[Upload page] -->|multipart file| API[POST /api/uploads]
  CLI[curl] --> API
  API -->|guard: token, size, count| V[parse JSON array]
  V -->|per item| ING[loadArticles with ingest pool]
  ING --> PG[(articles, ingest_events, quarantine, enrichment_jobs)]
  PG --> W[worker: claim, budget, breaker, provider]
  W --> PG
  UI -->|poll| ST[GET /api/uploads/:batchId]
  ST --> PG
```
Components
- `POST /api/uploads` (new route handler). Checks the shared upload token, content length against `UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES`, parses the file, rejects a non-array or an over-limit item count (`UPLOAD_MAX_ITEMS`) with 4xx and no rows written, then calls `loadArticles(items, "backfill", ingestPool, cfg)`. `backfill` keeps uploads out of the live freshness watermark (P3 honesty: not a live batch).
- `loadArticles` change: also return a per-item result list `{position, outcome, reason_codes, article_id}` (the data is already written to `ingest_events`). Keep the pure function shape (benchmarkable).
- `GET /api/uploads/:batchId` (new): reads `ingest_events` for the batch joined to `enrichment_jobs` states; read-only, can use the existing `app_read` pool (needs SELECT on `ingest_events` for `app_read`; today only `app_ingest` has it, so a one-line grant migration `0003`).
- Upload page (carma-ux): file picker, token field, report table, progress per article.
- Ingest pool in the web process: separate `createPool(...,"web-ingest")` with `app_ingest` credentials, used only by the upload route (D1).
- One in-flight upload per web instance (semaphore, 429 otherwise) so the ingest pool cannot starve search reads.

States per article: `received` (event) then `admitted | duplicate | quarantined`; admitted articles are searchable immediately (fresh before rich, P1) and enrichment jobs move `queued` to `done`, `deferred_budget` or `dead`.

Confidence and lineage: unchanged. Enrichment continues to write confidence, origin and method (P6, P7); each article traces to its upload through `ingest_events.batch_id` and `payload_sha256` (P8). Add `batch_kind`/source label `upload` only if D4 (not needed now) is accepted; otherwise the `batch_id` is the lineage.

Human touchpoint (P9): quarantined items from an upload appear in the existing quarantine review surface with their `batch_id`.

## 5. Options considered
O1 Where the write credential lives
1. Second pool in web using `app_ingest` (recommended): smallest change; mounts one more secret into web. Cost: web can now insert articles and events if compromised.
2. Dedicated ingest service/container with its own port, web proxies to it: strongest isolation, extra service, Compose change, more to run. Over the ADR 0001 scope.
3. Web stages the raw file into a table and a worker ingests it: keeps web read-only except one staging grant, adds new table, worker stage, and delays visibility (P1 cost).

O2 Sync vs async processing of the file
1. Synchronous in the request, bounded by caps (recommended): at about 4 queries per item, 1,000 items is a few to tens of seconds; the caller gets the full report. Cost: long request, ties up the ingest pool.
2. Accept (202) and process in the web process in background: route returns fast, but work is lost on restart and no recovery (P2).
3. Stage and process in a worker (see O1.3): durable, more build.

O3 Authentication
1. Shared upload token from a secret (`UPLOAD_TOKEN_FILE`), constant-time compare (recommended): the only write endpoint should not be open, and it spends LLM budget. Cost: token handling in the UI.
2. No auth, like the rest of the app: simplest, but anyone reaching the port can add data and spend budget.

O4 Idempotency and duplicates (no decision needed): reuse `(source, external_id)` skip plus content-hash flag; re-uploading the same file yields all `duplicate`, zero new jobs.

O5 Extensions: none needed. Core Postgres only.

## 6. Decisions needed
- D1 Write credential for the upload route: option 1 (second `app_ingest` pool in web), 2 (separate ingest service), or 3 (stage then worker). Recommend 1.
- D2 Processing model: sync bounded (recommend), or stage and worker. Linked to D1.
- D3 Authentication: shared token (recommend) or none.
- UNCONFIRMED defaults: `UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES=5 MiB`, `UPLOAD_MAX_ITEMS=1000`, uploads recorded as `backfill`, one upload at a time per instance.

## 7. Points of failure
| ID | Failure point | Mode and effect | Principle | Detection |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FP-1 | File is not valid JSON or not an array | Whole file rejected 400, nothing written; must say why | P3 | 4xx metric, report body |
| FP-2 | Oversized file or too many items | 413/422 before any write; no partial acceptance | P2 | reject counter by reason |
| FP-3 | Element invalid or non-object | Quarantined with reason code, others continue; position preserved | P3 | `ingest_events` count vs received |
| FP-4 | DB connection drops mid-file | Request fails after some items committed; caller must be able to resume safely | P2 | 5xx; re-upload is idempotent (N2) |
| FP-5 | Client disconnects mid-request | Server continues or aborts partway; batch partly applied without a report | P2 | batch event count vs expected; GET batch shows actual |
| FP-6 | Same file uploaded twice or concurrently | Concurrent identical items race on `(source, external_id)`; ON CONFLICT handles it, one admitted, one duplicate | P2 | duplicate count |
| FP-7 | Upload floods the LLM budget | 1,000 items queue jobs; budget caps spend and defers; lag shown | P2, ADR 0010 | deferred_budget count, budget banner |
| FP-8 | Upload starves search reads | Long upload holds the ingest pool and CPU | P1 | pool wait time, search p95 |
| FP-9 | Token missing/leaked/logged | Unauthorised writes; token in logs | security | 401 counter; log scrub test |
| FP-10 | Hostile article text (markup, injection, huge values, NULs, lone surrogates) | Existing sanitise/validate and ADR 0012 apply; unsafe items flagged | P2 | flags; sanity tests |
| FP-11 | Upload counted as live batch | Corrupts freshness watermark | P3 | batch_kind = backfill assertion |
| FP-12 | Outcome mismatch: received != admitted + duplicate + quarantined | Silent drop | P3 | per-request reconciliation, asserted in response and test |

## 8. Resilience design
| Dependency | Failure classes | Retry | Breaker | Bulkhead | Permanent failures | Degraded mode |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres (ingest pool) | transient: connection reset, 57P01/57P03, deadlock; permanent: constraint/validation (already quarantined per item) | No automatic retry inside the request; the caller re-sends (idempotent, FP-4). Per-item deadlock retry once is acceptable | None (pool errors surface as 503) | Separate ingest pool, one upload at a time, UPLOAD_MAX_ITEMS | Item errors recorded as `ingest_error` quarantine | 503 with `Retry-After`; reads keep working on the read pool |
| LLM providers | unchanged: worker retry, breaker and budget (ADR 0010, existing `src/worker/*`) | existing | existing | existing worker concurrency | dead-letter existing | Articles searchable, enrichment shows queued/deferred, confidence "none yet" |
| Client | disconnect, slow upload | none | n/a | request timeout and body limit | n/a | Partial effects visible through `GET /api/uploads/:batchId` |

## 9. Hot paths
| ID | Path | Why hot | Expected load | What needs a human | Measurement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HP-1 | `ingestOne` per upload item | 4+ queries per item, sequential | up to 1,000 items per request | Decide batch limits and whether to batch inserts after measuring; inspect transaction scope | items/s and request p95 for 1,000 items on the small DB profile |
| HP-2 | JSON parse of up to 5 MiB in the web process | Blocks the event loop | one at a time | Confirm limit vs memory limit of the container (mem_limit in compose) | peak RSS, event-loop lag |
| HP-3 | Batch status query | Join events to jobs for a batch | polling every few seconds | Review plan on `events_batch_idx` | query p95 |

carma-benchmark candidates: HP-1 (completeness `received = accounted for`, plus throughput).

## 10. Telemetry starting points
`upload_requests_total{outcome}`, `upload_rejected_total{reason}`, `upload_items_total{outcome}`, `upload_duration_seconds`, ingest pool wait/usage, in-flight upload gauge, 401/429 counts, batch reconciliation mismatch counter (must stay 0), deferred_budget jobs for upload batches, event-loop lag, plus existing worker, queue age and breaker signals. Log batch_id, byte size, item count, never the file contents or token.

## 11. Principle alignment
| Principle | Serves | Costs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P1 | Admitted articles searchable before enrichment | Sync upload holds the request |
| P2 | Per-item transactions, transactional enqueue, idempotent re-upload | No resumable upload; caller re-sends |
| P3 | Every element has an outcome, whole-file rejects are loud | Upload caps may refuse legitimate big files |
| P6/P7/P8 | Unchanged enrichment confidence, batch_id lineage | None |
| P9 | Quarantine review covers uploads | Review UI scope unchanged |

## 12. Downstream handoff
- carma-searchability: no new query needs; uploaded articles are searchable through existing paths. Run only if routing wants confirmation. Skip suggested.
- carma-data-sanity: apply. Untrusted file: size and count caps, content-type, JSON depth, filename handling, injection into LLM (ADR 0012), token handling.
- carma-dba: small. Grant `SELECT` on `ingest_events` to `app_read` (or a status function), ingest pool in web, per-batch index check; possibly a `status_batch(batch_id)` SQL function.
- carma-telemetry: apply (section 10).
- carma-ux: apply. Upload page, report table, per-article progress.
- carma-devops: apply. Mount `app_ingest_password` and `UPLOAD_TOKEN` secret into web (`ops/init-secrets.sh`, `compose.yaml`), request body limits, container memory.
- carma-backend-testing: apply (FP-1..FP-12, reconciliation, idempotent re-upload, fault injection on the DB).
- carma-plan: last.
- carma-benchmark after code: HP-1. carma-review: keep `ingestOne` untouched and the route handler thin.

## 13. Open questions and assumptions
- UNCONFIRMED: caps 5 MiB / 1,000 items; `backfill` kind; single in-flight upload; token auth.
- UNCONFIRMED: whether Next.js route handlers in this version stream or buffer `request.formData()` and its default size limits (check docs before coding).
- Is the upload meant for operators only (internal) or for external clients? Affects D3.
- Should an upload file be retained after processing? Assumed no (only per-item payload hashes, quarantine payload per ADR 0011).

# ADR-0019: Upload route writes through a second app_ingest pool in web and processes the file synchronously under caps

## Context and problem statement
The web service holds only the read-only `app_read` credential. A JSON upload needs to insert articles, events and jobs. Architect 0002 D1 and D2.

## Decision drivers
- P2 reliable (per-item transactions, transactional enqueue, idempotent re-upload)
- ADR 0001: assignment scope, do not gold-plate
- P1: admitted articles searchable before enrichment

## Considered options
1. Second `app_ingest` pool in web, synchronous under caps (chosen)
2. Stage the file in a table, worker ingests
3. Separate ingest service

## Decision outcome
Chosen option 1. The upload route alone uses the `app_ingest` pool (never the read routes). Caps `UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES` and `UPLOAD_MAX_ITEMS` (defaults 5 MiB, 1000, UNCONFIRMED) bound the request; one upload in flight per web instance.

### Consequences
- Good: reuses `loadArticles`; smallest change; full per-article report in the response.
- Bad: web can now write if compromised; long requests tie up the ingest pool; no resumable upload.
- Risks and how we will notice them: FP-4, FP-5, FP-8; HP-1 measurement.

### Confirmation
Backend tests for FP-1..FP-12, benchmark of HP-1, pool wait metric.

## Pros and cons of the options
1. Simple and fast to build; widens web privileges.
2. Durable and isolated; new table, worker stage, delayed visibility.
3. Strongest isolation; most Compose work.

Chosen option 1. The upload route alone uses the `app_ingest` pool (never the read routes). Caps `UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES` and `UPLOAD_MAX_ITEMS` (defaults 5 MiB, 1000, UNCONFIRMED) bound the request; one upload in flight per web instance.

### Consequences
- Good: reuses `loadArticles`; smallest change; full per-article report in the response.
- Bad: web can now write if compromised; long requests tie up the ingest pool; no resumable upload.
- Risks and how we will notice them: FP-4, FP-5, FP-8; HP-1 measurement.

### Confirmation
Backend tests for FP-1..FP-12, benchmark of HP-1, pool wait metric.

## Pros and cons of the options
1. Simple and fast to build; widens web privileges.
2. Durable and isolated; new table, worker stage, delayed visibility.
3. Strongest isolation; most Compose work.
